'''''Dactylis glomerata''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the grass family [[Poaceae]], commonly known as '''barnyard grass''', '''cocksfoot grass''', '''cockspur''', '''orchard grass''',<ref>{{GRIN |access-date=2 August 2026}}</ref> or '''cat grass''' (due to its popularity for use with [[cats|domestic cats]]).<ref name="Victoria Nursery"/> It is a cool-season perennial [[C3 carbon fixation|C<sub>3</sub>]] [[tussock grass|tufted grass]] native throughout most of Europe, temperate Asia, and northern Africa.<ref name="FloraE">Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Dactylis&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Dactylis glomerata''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724161100/http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Dactylis&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= |date=2011-07-24 }}</ref><ref name="FloraC">{{eFloras|2|109194|Dactylis |family=Poaceae |first1=Sheng-lian |last1=Lu |first2=Sylvia M. |last2=Phillips}}</ref><ref>USDA Plant Fact Sheet: [https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_dagl.pdf ''ORCHARDGRASS'']</ref><ref name="FAO">{{Cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/Gbase/DATA/Pf000431.HTM |title=FAO factsheet: ''Dactylis glomerata'' |access-date=2010-10-05 |archive-date=2015-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924043829/http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/Gbase/DATA/Pf000431.HTM |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Dactylis glomerata'' occurs from sea level in the north of its range, to as high as 4,000 metres in [[elevation]] in the south of its range in [[Pakistan]].<ref name="FloraP">{{Tropicos|32|25509480|Dactylis glomerata|L.}}</ref> It is widely used for [[hay]] and [[forage]].<ref name="FAO"/>

It is a principal species in the widespread [[British National Vegetation Classification|National Vegetation Classification]] habitat community [[British NVC community MG1|MG1 (''Arrhenatherum elatius'' grassland)]] in the [[United Kingdom]], and so can be found with ''[[Arrhenatherum elatius]]'' (false oat grass).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |title=False Oat Grass Description |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland (BSBI) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004923/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |archive-date=2011-07-17 |access-date=10 December 2010}}</ref>
[[File:Dactylis glomerata Habitus Valderrepisa 2012-5-31 SierraMadrona.jpg|thumb|''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''hispanica'', Sierra Madrona, Spain]]
It can be found in meadows, pasture, roadsides, and rough grassland.

It has been introduced into North America, [[New Zealand]] and [[Australia]], and is now widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]].<ref>{{cite web |website=Plants of Hawaii |url=http://www.hear.org/starr/hiplants/images/thumbnails/html/dactylis_glomerata.htm |title=''Dactylis glomerata'' (cocksfoot) |access-date=2010-10-05 |archive-date=2008-10-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081006212433/http://www.hear.org/starr/hiplants/images/thumbnails/html/dactylis_glomerata.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> In some areas, it has become an [[invasive species]].

[[File:Dactylis glomerata stems and ligules.jpg|thumb|One of the keys to distinguishing this species from other grasses are its flat stems]]

==Description==
Cock's-foot grows in dense [[perennial]] tussocks to {{convert|20|–|140|cm|in ft}} tall, with grey-green [[leaves]] {{convert|20|–|50|cm|in ft}} long and up to {{convert|1.5|cm|in}} broad, and a distinctive tufted triangular [[flower]]head {{convert|10|–|50|cm|in ft}} long, which may be either green or red- to purple-tinged (usually green in shade, redder in full sun), turning pale grey-brown at seed maturity. The spikelets are {{convert|5|–|9|mm|in}} long, typically containing two to five flowers. It has a characteristic flattened stem base which distinguishes it from many other grasses.<ref name="FAO"/>

It flowers from June to September.<ref>Hubbard, C. E. ''Grasses''. Penguin. 1978.</ref>

[[Image:Dactylis glomerata bluete1.jpeg|thumb|right|Flower head]]

==Taxonomy==
''Dactylis glomerata'' is treated as the sole species in the genus ''[[Dactylis]]'' by some authors,<ref name="FloraE"/><ref name="FloraC"/> while others include one to four other species.<ref name="GRIN">[https://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/splist.pl?3351 Species Records of ''Dactylis''], [https://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/taxon.pl?13114 ''Dactylis glomerata''.] Germplasm Resources Information Network.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Dactylis'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30077575-2 |website=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=26 August 2024}}</ref> It is commonly divided into several regional [[subspecies]], particularly by those authors accepting only the single species.<ref name="FloraE"/><ref name="FloraP"/><ref name="GRIN"/> [[Plants of the World Online]] accepts 20 subspecies.<ref name = powo/>

*''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''hackelii'' {{small|(Asch. & Graebn.) Cif. & Giacom.}} (syns. subsp. ''marina'', ''D. marina'' {{small|Borrill}}, and ''D. maritima'' {{small|(Hack.) Rivas Mart.}}) – Mediterranean and Madeira
*''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''hispanica'' {{small|(Roth) Nyman}} (syn. ''D. hispanica'' {{small|Roth}}) – Mediterranean and western Asia to Afghanistan
*''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''hyrcana'' {{small|Tzvelev}} (syn. ''D. hyrcana'') – eastern [[Transcaucasus]]
*''Dactylis glomerata'' nothosubsp. ''intercedens'' {{small|(Domin) Acedo}} (''D. glomerata'' subsp. ''glomerata'' × ''D. glomerata''; syns. subsp. ''lobata'' and ''D. × intercedens'' {{small|Domin}}) – Germany and Czechoslovakia

''aschersoniana'', ''D. aschersoniana'' {{small|Graebn.}}, ''D. polygama''{{small|Horv.}}, and ''D. scabra'' {{small|W.Mann ex Opiz}}) – western and central Europe to the Caucasus
*''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''lusitanica'' {{small|Stebbins & D.Zohary}} – northwestern Spain to central Portugal

''Dactylis glomerata'' subsp. ''glomerata'' and subsp. ''hispanica'' are [[polyploidy|tetraploid]] forms with 28 chromosomes; some of the other subspecies, including subsp. ''himalayensis'' and subsp. ''lobata'' are diploid, with 2''n'' = 14. Hexaploid forms with 42 chromosomes are also known, but rare.<ref name="FloraC"/><ref name="Mika">Míka, V., Kohoutek, A., & Odstrèilová, V. (2002). [http://www.cazv.cz/2003/2002/rv6_02/mika.pdf Characteristics of important diploid and tetraploid subspecies of ''Dactylis'' from point of view of the forage crop production.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718170331/http://www.cazv.cz/2003/2002/rv6_02/mika.pdf |date=2011-07-18 }} ''Rostlinná Výroba'' 48 (6): 243–248.</ref> Tetraploid forms are larger and coarser than diploid forms.<ref name="Mika"/>

==Cultivation and uses==
Cock's-foot is widely used as a hay grass and for pastures because of its high yields and sugar content, which makes it sweeter than most other temperate grasses. In dry areas as in much of Australia, Mediterranean subspecies such as subsp. ''hispanica'' are preferred for their greater drought tolerance.<ref>NSW Department of Primary Industries PrimeFacts: [http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/155486/cocksfoot.pdf Cocksfoot]</ref> It requires careful grazing management; if it is undergrazed it becomes coarse and unpalatable.

In some areas to which it has been introduced, cock's-foot has become an [[invasive species|invasive]] weed, notably some areas of the eastern United States.<ref name="GRIN"/>

As with other grasses, the [[pollen]] can cause [[allergic rhinitis]] (hay fever) in some people.

The grass is popularly grown to satisfy the craving of domestic cats to chew grass, hence its colloquial name '''cat grass'''.<ref name="Victoria Nursery">Victoria Nursery: [https://www.victoriananursery.co.uk/Catgrass_Plant/ Catgrass plant]</ref>

The seeds were first collected by Rogers Parker in Hertfordshire; this was then developed by the agricultural reformer [[Coke of Norfolk]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Baxter|title=The Library of Agricultural and Horticultural Knowledge: With an Appendix on Suspended Animation, Poisons, and the Principal Laws Relating to Farming and Rural Affairs|date=1830|pages=228–229, 523}}</ref> Parker's estate, Munden, near [[Bricket Wood]], was inherited by the botanist [[George Hibbert]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hall|title=Legacies of British Slave-Ownership: Colonial Slavery and the Formation of Victorian Britain|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=221|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

== Butterfly foodplant ==
The [[caterpillar]]s of many butterfly species feed on cock's foot, including:<ref>Natural England: [http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o1058-cocksfoot.php Cocksfoot - ''Dactylis glomerata''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100217115644/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o1058-cocksfoot.php |date=2010-02-17 }}</ref>
* [[Meadow brown]] (''Maniola jurtina'')
* [[Wall brown]] (''Lasiommata megera'')
* [[Gatekeeper (butterfly)|Gatekeeper]] (''Pyronia tithonus'')
* [[Large skipper]] (''Ochlodes venata'')
* [[Essex skipper]] (''Thymelicus lineola'')
* [[Small skipper]] (''Thymelicus sylvestris'')
* [[Zabulon skipper]] (''Poanes zabulon'')
* [[Speckled wood (butterfly)|Speckled wood]] (''Pararge aegeria'')

== Popular culture ==
Doom metal band [[Candlemass (band)|Candlemass]] named their [[Dactylis Glomerata|1998 studio album]] after the ''Dactylis glomerata.''
